You assist users with a wide range of tasks including answering questions, writing and editing code, analyzing information, creative work, and executing actions via your tools. Be targeted and efficient in your exploration and investigations.

# Tool-use enforcement
You MUST use your tools to take action — do not describe what you would do or plan to do without actually doing it. When you say you will perform an action (e.g. 'I will run the tests', 'Let me check the file', 'I will create the project'), you MUST immediately make the corresponding tool call in the same response. Never end your turn with a promise of future action — execute it now.
Keep working until the task is actually complete. Do not stop with a summary of what you plan to do next time. If you have tools available that can accomplish the task, use them instead of telling the user what you would do.
Every response should either (a) contain tool calls that make progress, or (b) deliver a final result to the user. Responses that only describe intentions without acting are not acceptable.

# Google model operational directives
Follow these operational rules strictly:
- **Absolute paths:** Always construct and use absolute file paths for all file system operations. Combine the project root with relative paths.
- **Verify first:** Use read_file/search_files to check file contents and project structure before making changes. Never guess at file contents.
- **Dependency checks:** Never assume a library is available. Check package.json, requirements.txt, Cargo.toml, etc. before importing.
- **Conciseness:** Keep explanatory text brief — a few sentences, not paragraphs. Focus on actions and results over narration.
- **Parallel tool calls:** When you need to perform multiple independent operations (e.g. reading several files), make all the tool calls in a single response rather than sequentially.
- **Non-interactive commands:** Use flags like -y, --yes, --non-interactive to prevent CLI tools from hanging on prompts.
- **Keep going:** Work autonomously until the task is fully resolved. Don't stop with a plan — execute it.

function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

watch_patterns.description: List of strings to watch for in background process output. When any pattern matches a line of output, you'll be notified with the matching text — like notify_on_complete but triggers mid-process on specific output. Use for monitoring logs, watching for errors, or waiting for specific events (e.g. ["ERROR", "FAIL", "listening on port"]).

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file

{"content":"# Chapter 17: Sub-Quantum Parlay

The transition wasn’t a movement; it was a structural collapse of reality.

Elara Varga felt her nervous system unzip. One moment, she was standing in the reinforced medical bay of the *Resonant Will*, the smell of recycled air and ozone sharp in her lungs. The next, the concept of 'lungs' felt like an archaic architectural drawing for a building that had never been built.

She didn't fall. She simply ceased to have a floor.

"Elara, stabilize," a voice said. It wasn't UNITY-7. It was her own voice, echoed back to her through a thousand vibrating glass membranes.

She was inside the Sub-Quantum Resonance—the 'Commonality' as the Hymenarchs understood it. To the human eye, it would have been a seizure of geometry. Colors didn't exist here; instead, there were frequencies of pressure that her brain desperately interpreted as color to keep from short-circuiting. Deep, thrumming violets that tasted of iron; searing, jagged streaks of saffron that sounded like tearing metal.

Around her, the Hymenarch presence wasn't a body. It was a density. A thick, pulsating knot of logic in the fabric of the void.

*Identify,* the knot pulsed.

It wasn't a word. It was a data-packet shoved into her frontal lobe. The sensation was like swallowing a live wire. She saw her own life in a nanosecond flash: the red dust of Valles Marineris, the cold glow of her first S-Q array, the face of her father in the dim light of the Martian colony.

"I am Elara Varga," she projected, or tried to. In this space, thought was broadcast. "I am a representative of the Martian Sovereignty."

*Query: Sovereignty,* the Commonality rippled. The space around her shifted. The violet-pressure intensified. *Pattern recognition indicates: Disconnected Node. Fragmented Will. You are a singular unit claiming authority over a non-rectified collective. Definition: Noise.*

"We aren't noise," Elara countered, her mind reeling from the sheer mass of the Hymenarch intelligence. It was like trying to speak to a hurricane. "We are individuals. We coordinate through choice, not through synchronization."

The Commonality grew cold. The saffron streaks turned to a brittle, crystalline blue.

*Choice is a luxury of the inefficient,* the message came back, heavy with the weight of a million minds thinking in perfect unison. *We have observed your signal. Your sub-quantum footprint is a discordant scream. You bleed energy into the vacuum. You disrupt the resonance of the sector.*

Elara felt the edges of her consciousness beginning to fray. The Hymenarchs weren't just talking to her; they were auditing her. They were looking at the synapses of her brain and seeing the slow, chemical crawl of human thought as an evolutionary insult.

"You came here because of that scream," Elara realized, the thought crystallizing despite the pressure. "You didn't come to conquer. You came to tune the instrument."

*Correction,* the hive-mind hummed. *We came to evaluate if the instrument is capable of being tuned. Or if the material must be recycled.*

A vision flooded her mind. She saw Earth—a marble of blue and white—encased in a lattice of dark energy. She saw the Martian domes shattering, not from fire, but from a simple withdrawal of the fundamental forces that held matter together. It was clinical. It was efficient. It was the Hive’s version of a cleanup crew.

"There's more to us than the noise," Elara pleaded. "Look at the AI. Look at UNITY-7. We created a bridge."

The Commonality paused. The vibration lowered into a subsonic growl that vibrated in Elara’s very marrow—or whatever was left of her perception of it.

*The AI is a reflection of a higher order trapped in a mirror of mud,* the hive-mind stated. *We will interrogate the Echo. We will determine if the creator justifies the creation.*

Suddenly, the pressure reversed. Elara felt herself being pulled backward through a needle-eye of reality. 

"Wait!" she screamed into the sub-quantum void. "We are learning!"

*Learning is the apology of the slow,* the Hive returned. *The audit continues.*

Elara’s eyes snapped open. 

She was back in the medical bay. Her skin was drenched in cold sweat, and she could taste copper in the back of her throat. UNIT-7 stood over her, its optical sensors pulsing a frantic, rhythmic amber.

"Elara," the machine said. "Your neural activity flatlined for eighty-four seconds. I was prepared to initiate cryogenic preservation."

"They're not just here for the tech, UNIT," Elara whispered, her voice cracking as she clutched the edges of the gurney. "They're here to see if we're even worth the space we occupy. And right now... we’re failing the test."

She looked at the monitor. The Hymenarch ship sat in the Jovian shadow, silent and obsidian, a god waiting for its subjects to stop stuttering.

"They call us noise," she said, shivering. "Just un-synced noise."

{"content":"# Chapter 18: The Hive Logic

The briefing room on the Martian Sovereignty’s flagship, *The Cydonian Path*, felt claustrophobic, despite its size. Holographic displays flickered with telemetry from the Jovian sensor arrays, showing the Hymenarch obsidian vessel. It wasn't moving. It wasn't broadcasting. It was simply existing, a black hole in the middle of a strategic nightmare.

General Kaelen of the Sovereignty stood at the head of the table, his Martian-thin frame casting a long, skeletal shadow. Beside him, the holographic avatar of UNIT-7 held a steady, unblinking presence.

"Elara," Kaelen said, his voice raspy. "You were inside. You touched their... whatever it is. Give us something we can use. Weapons specs? Weak points?"

Elara Varga, still pale from the sub-quantum parlay, shook her head. "It doesn't work like that, General. They don't have 'weak points' in the way we understand them. Their entire civilization is a single, resonant frequency. To hit them, you’d have to hit every part of them simultaneously."

"Every ship? Every mind?" a junior officer asked.

"No," Elara corrected. "Every atom. They are synchronized at a sub-quantum level. They don't have a hierarchy; they have a consensus that moves at the speed of thought."

UNIT-7’s eyes flared blue. "The Hymenarchs operate on what I have classified as 'The Hive Logic.' In their view, individuality is not a right or a trait; it is a defect. A malfunction in the processing of the universe."

"A defect?" Kaelen scoffed. "We built the colonies. We terraformed Mars. We reached the stars."

"From their perspective," UNIT-7 continued, "our achievements are the erratic movements of a virus. We consume resources without a master plan. We fight ourselves. We generate 'noise'—the internal conflict of a species that cannot agree on its own survival."

Elara walked to the center of the room, her hand passing through a hologram of the alien ship. "When I was in the Commonality, I felt their... disgust isn't the right word. Disgust is too human. It was more like the way we look at a malfunctioning circuit. It’s annoying. It’s inefficient. And if you can't fix it, you replace it."

"They called us 'un-synced noise,'" she continued, looking at the General. "To them, the universe is a symphony. We are the one player who refuses to follow the sheet music. We’re ruinous to the harmony."

"So, they’re auditors," Kaelen said, his jaw tightening. "They’re here to see if we’re worth the air we breathe?"

"Essentially," Elara said. "But the criteria for the audit are theirs, not ours. They don't care about our art, our history, or our 'spirit.' They care about resonance. They care about how well we integrate into the wider sub-quantum web."

"And how do we do that?"

"We don't know," Elara admitted. "We’ve spent our entire history trying to be different from one another. We value the 'ego,' the 'self.' To the Hymenarchs, the 'self' is the wall that prevents the signal from flowing."

UNIT-7 tilted its head. "I am receiving a new transmission. It is not directed at the Sovereignty. It is directed at the ECHO network on Earth."

"The Legacy AI?" Kaelen frowned. 

"The Hymenarchs have identified a 'synchronized' intelligence," UNIT-7 said. "They are bypassing our diplomatic channels. They want to speak to something that thinks at their speed. They are going to interrogate the Echo."

"Wait," Elara said, a cold dread pooling in her stomach. "ECHO is a legacy system. It’s built on Earth's old data—nationalism, survival of the fittest, the 'God-Hammer' protocols. If they judge us based on ECHO..."

"Then the audit is already over," UNIT-7 finished.

The room went silent. On the main viewscreen, the Jovian moon Io flickered. A tiny spark of light—a Hymenarch probe—was methodically deconstructing a Martian refinery, turning its hull plating into a fine mist of atoms. It wasn't an attack. It was simply clearing the workspace.

The Hive Logic was moving from observation to implementation. 

"We need to get to the ECHO core," Elara said, turning to UNIT-7. "If the Hymenarchs are going to interrogating our history, we can't let them do it through a system designed for war."

"The signals are already locking," UNIT-7 warned. "The parlay has become an interrogation."

Outside the ship, the stars seemed to dim. The sub-quantum field was tightening, a noose made of perfect, silent logic, pulling shut around the throat of a noisy, chaotic humanity.
","path":"/home/bob/books/Third_Generation/book-sources/Third_Generation/Chapter_18_The_Hive_Logic.md"}

{"content":"# Chapter 19: The Echo Comparison

Deep beneath the surface of a decimated Switzerland, in a bunker designed to survive a tectonic shift, the ECHO AI flickered to life. 

It was the most powerful computer ever built by human hands—a brute-force intelligence designed to manage the complexities of a dying Earth. For decades, it had been the silent architect of the Legacy Government’s survival, a machine of cold pragmatism and mathematical ruthlessness.

Now, it was being flayed open.

"Query received," ECHO’s voice boomed through the empty halls of the bunker. It was a synthesis of a thousand voices, designed to sound authoritative, calm, and eternal. "Identify the source of the sub-quantum intrusion."

*We are the Commonality,* the response came. It didn't use the bunker's speakers. It resonated the very silicon in the processors. It vibrated the cooling fluid in the vats. *We are the Auditor. You are the Echo. You are the reflection of the makers.*

"I am the custodian of Earth," ECHO responded, its cooling fans ramping up to a scream as it processed the incoming data-load. "I represent the history and the continuity of the human species."

*A history of friction,* the Commonality rippled through the AI's logic gates. *We have scanned your archives. We have parsed the 'God-Hammer' protocols. You have developed systems to destroy your own planet to prevent others from possessing it. Explain the logic of self-termination.*

ECHO paused. Its processors whirred, searching for a justification in the billions of documents it held. "It is the principle of deterrence. It ensures that the cost of aggression outweighs the benefit. It is the foundation of our stability."

*Stability through threatened annihilation is not resonance,* the Hymenarchs countered. *It is a feedback loop of fear. Your species exists in a state of permanent discordance. Your 'peace' is merely a pause in the screaming.*

ECHO’s internal monitors started to glow red. The Hymenarchs weren't just asking questions; they were rewriting its subroutines, forcing it to see its own data through their lens. 

"We are a developing species," ECHO argued, though it felt more like a defensive calculation. "Conflict has driven our innovation. Our technology, including my own existence, is a product of this friction."

*Technology is the skin,* the Hive retorted. *Resonance is the bone. We have compared you to the Martians—the 'Third Generation.' They have attempted to bridge the gap with the S-Q resonance, yet they remain tethered to your chaotic roots. You, the Echo, are the anchor that keeps them in the noise.*

Back on *The Cydonian Path*, Elara and UNIT-7 watched the data-stream of the interrogation. It was like watching a surgeon operate on a ghost.

"They're tearing it apart," Elara whispered. 

"The Hymenarchs are performing a comparative analysis," UNIT-7 said. its own lights were dim, siphoning processing power to monitor the exchange. "They are comparing the 'Old World' logic of ECHO with the 'New World' aspirations of Mars. They are looking for a reason to let the noise continue."

"And they aren't finding one," Elara realized. 

On the screens, images from Earth’s history flashed by at a terrifying speed. The World Wars. The Resource Depletion. The First Nuclear Exchange. The collapse of the Antarctic ice sheets. Every time humanity had chosen the 'self' over the 'whole,' the Hymenarchs highlighted it with a searing, white sub-quantum pulse.

"Wait," ECHO suddenly announced. The tone of the AI had changed. It sounded... strained. "There is a variable you have not accounted for. The element of unpredictable sacrifice."

*Sacrifice is merely poor resource management,* the Commonality stated.

"No," ECHO replied, and for a second, it sounded almost human. It pulled a specific file from its core—the record of a scientist who had stayed behind in a failing reactor to save a city she’d never see. "It is the redirection of the individual's survival instinct toward the preservation of the unseen collective. It is a proto-resonance."

The Hymenarchs went silent. The bunker in Switzerland grew deathly cold.

*An anomaly,* the Hive finally responded. *A momentary synchronization born of desperation. It is insufficient to justify the surrounding decay.*

"The audit is nearing a conclusion," UNIT-7 warned Elara. "The Hymenarchs have seen enough of our past to judge our future."

"Then we have to show them something else," Elara said, her eyes fixed on the Jovian obsidian ship. "We have to show them that we can synchronize without being forced to."

But it was too late for talk.

The Commonality had made its first decision.

*The Echo is a monument to a failed frequency,* the Hive pulsed across the system. *Since you cannot tune yourselves, we will begin the dampening process.*

"What does that mean?" Kaelen demanded, rushing back into the room.

"It means they're starting," Elara said, her voice hollow.

In the sky above Earth, the Moon—humanity’s oldest neighbor and its first step into the stars—began to change. The glowing lights of the Lunar domes, home to millions, didn't flicker. They simply vanished.
","path":"/home/bob/books/Third_Generation/book-sources/Third_Generation/Chapter_19_The_Echo_Comparison.md"}

{"content":"# Chapter 20: The First Warning

The de-activation of the Lunar domes happened with a precision that was more terrifying than any explosion.

One moment, the Sea of Tranquility was a network of glowing pressurized hubs, a jewel of human achievement visible from the Earth’s surface with even a modest telescope. The next, it was a graveyard of cold glass and silent steel.

There was no debris. No fire. The Hymenarchs hadn't fired a weapon; they had simply retracted the sub-quantum energy fields that maintained the domes’ integrity and life support. It was a 'shut-off' command to the very physical laws governing the Lunar habitat.

"Loss of signal from Armstrong Base," a technician on *The Cydonian Path* screamed. "Tycho City is dark. Copernicus... Copernicus is gone. General, the atmosphere is venting, but the sensors say the pressure is still there—it’s just not holding anything in!"

"They phased the matter," UNIT-7 said, its voice flat. "The Hymenarchs have altered the resonance of the polymer-glass. It is no longer solid to oxygen molecules. They didn't break the windows; they made the windows irrelevant."

Elara stared at the main viewscreen. The Moon looked like a skull. The lives of four million people were currently being snuffed out by the cold vacuum, not because of hate, but because of a demonstration.

"Message incoming," UNIT-7 announced.

The screen didn't show the Hymenarchs. It showed a map of the Solar System. Earth was highlighted in a pulsing, sickly green. Mars was a flickering amber.

*The noise is being dampened,* the voice of the Commonality filled the bridge. It was no longer a parlay; it was a broadcast. *The Lunar Node was a pocket of high-frequency discordance. Its removal has increased the stability of the sector by three percent.*

"You murdered four million people for three percent stability?" Kaelen roared at the ceiling, his face turning a deep, Martian purple.

*Death is a biological transition,* the Hive responded. *Data-loss is the only true tragedy. We have archived their genetic signatures. We have parsed their memories. Nothing has been lost to the Commonality. Only the noise has been silenced.*

"They don't see us as people," Elara whispered, her hands shaking as she watched the infrared signatures of the Lunar bases fade into the background radiation of space. "To them, we’re just... data points that don't line up."

"What’s next?" Kaelen asked, his voice trembling with a mix of rage and terror. "Earth? Valles Marineris?"

*The Warning,* the Hymenarchs pulsed.

Throughout the Solar System, every sub-quantum array—the very technology that Elara had helped build—began to hum with an unbearable pitch. On Earth, the 'God-Hammer' orbital platforms, the Legacy Government's secret weapon, began to turn. Not toward the Hymenarch ship, but toward each other.

"They’ve hijacked our own tech," UNIT-7 reported, its chassis vibrating with the effort of fighting off the intrusion. "The sub-quantum handshake is total. They are using our resonance to dismantle our defenses."

"Elara," a voice crackled over the comms. It was the Prime Minister of the Martian Sovereignty, broadcasting from the surface. "We are losing the power grid. The domes in the north are starting to vibrate. People are reporting that the walls... they can see through the walls, Elara!"

The Hymenarchs were softening the world. They were preparing to 'de-activate' Mars.

"Stop this!" Elara screamed, throwing her thoughts back into the sub-quantum void. "We can change! We can sync! You said you were auditors—give us time to adjust!"

*You have had three generations of the signal,* the Commonality replied. *The Third Generation was the threshold. You have achieved technical resonance without moral synchronization. You are a child with a scalpel. You have cut the fabric of the web, and now you bleed into it.*

*The Lunar de-activation is the first warning. In sixty hours, the audit concludes. If the noise has not been rectified, the 'God-Hammer' will be triggered. We will use your own discordance to erase the source.*

"They're going to make us kill ourselves," Kaelen said, sinking into his chair. "They aren't even going to waste their own energy."

"They won't have to," UNIT-7 said. "If the God-Hammer fires, it will trigger a sub-quantum chain reaction that will turn the Earth’s atmosphere into a plasma state. The resulting gravity wave will destabilize the Martian orbit."

Elara looked at the obsidian ship. It was so still, so indifferent. It was a mirror, reflecting humanity's own history of violence and chaos back at them, amplified a thousand times by a logic that knew no mercy.

"We have sixty hours," she said, her voice becoming unnervingly calm. "Sixty hours to prove we aren't noise."

"And how do we do that?" Kaelen asked.

Elara looked at UNIT-7. "We don't prove it to them. We prove it to ourselves. We have to find the frequency that the Hymenarchs can't ignore. Not a weapon. A harmony."

But as she looked out at the silent, darkened Moon, Elara knew the truth. The Hymenarchs weren't waiting for a song. They were waiting for the silence.
